method: The linear coefficient of thermal expansion, α, is the fractional change in length per kelvin, so its SI unit is the reciprocal kelvin; a length L changes by α L ΔT over a temperature interval ΔT. This page converts α only: it applies no temperature, length, strain or stress, and it recommends no material. Every listed unit reduces to 1/K by one exact factor. A reciprocal degree Celsius carries the same factor as 1/K, because a temperature interval of one kelvin is one degree Celsius. A reciprocal degree Fahrenheit is 9/5 per kelvin, since a Fahrenheit degree interval is 5/9 K, which is the factor behind both the ppm/°F and µin/(in·°F) forms. A part per million per kelvin is exactly 1e-6/K, and a micrometre per metre-kelvin is the same factor because a micrometre per metre is 1e-6; a micro-inch per inch-degree Fahrenheit is 1e-6/°F, so 1.8e-6/K. A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every pair round trips, and the headline also states the change of a one-metre length per kelvin in micrometres, which is α × 1e6. Negative coefficients are accepted because some materials contract as they warm — zirconium tungstate, and water between 0 and 4 °C — so the input may carry a minus sign, while a magnitude of 10 per kelvin or more is outside the supported range and is refused. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally grouped in thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, exponent form is refused. Results carry six significant digits with trailing zeros trimmed and thousands grouped, and a magnitude below 1e-6 or from 1e12 up is written in exponential form. The reference table holds round coefficients from 1 to 23 ppm/K in two systems. Coefficients vary with temperature, alloy and direction, so a handbook figure is only as good as the range it is quoted for. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
